7.0.s.en: 1. "How beautiful are thy steps (thy feet) with shoes, O prince's daughter!" [1].

7.0.0.en: He calls her "prince's daughter" since she is related to God, born of water and the Spirit as a daughter of the heavenly King. Therefore she was called in the psalm (Ps 45:13) "the king's daughter." Though in her origin (after the Fall) she was lowly and despised, by her relation to God she bore a royal origin.

7.0.1.en: The bride had already praised her Bridegroom (Song 5:11-15), describing Him beginning from the head down to the feet, for she was dazzled by His majesty and glory, so she spoke of the head, which represents His person, then progressed to praise even His feet. But the Bridegroom, in praising the bride, begins with the feet, or her steps, until He describes the head, and that for two reasons: first, that He wants to confirm that the secret of her beauty is her steps, or her walking in the royal way, that is, her return in repentance to the Bridegroom, the secret of her life. And the second reason is that He wanted to give greater honor to the members that seem to be without honor (1 Cor 12:23-24).

7.0.2.en: As for His speaking of the "shoes," it refers to the Church - as a congregation or as members - having been shod with the Gospel of peace (Eph 6:15), as though the Bridegroom concentrated at the beginning of describing her on her evangelical steps... she walks the way of the Bridegroom Himself, practicing her evangelical life full of peace. This is the secret of her spiritual beauty, that she knew the way and entered it! Thus she also bears witness to her Bridegroom, as the Apostle Paul says: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" (Rom 10:15). And the saying of the prophet Isaiah: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" (Isa 52:7), and the saying of Nahum the prophet: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the king shall no more pass through thee" (Nah 1:15).

7.0.3.en: When the soul is shod with the word of the Lord she becomes a bearer of the secret of her inner peace and of the peace of others, so she preaches the word of salvation and proclaims the kingdom of God declared on the Cross, and pours joy into the hearts of believers; thereby they obtain the spirit of victory and triumph over the destroyer.

7.1.s.en: 2. "The joints of thy thighs are like jewels (chains), the work of the hands of a cunning workman" [1].

7.1.0.en: The thighs carry the body and help it to move, therefore the joints of the thighs signify the unity of the holy Church in Christ Jesus through love. Regarding this the Apostle says: "speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ: from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love" (Eph 4:15-16). Through this unity the body grows and is strengthened (Col 2:19), so the mission of the Church is accomplished.

7.1.1.en: This unity, like chains, binds humanity together despite its differences in language, race, and cultures, and also binds the generations together, so the Church bears the catholic spirit on the level of place (in all the world) and the level of time (across the generations)... and it is the work of the hands of a skilled craftsman, namely the Holy Spirit, the giver of fellowship.

7.2.s.en: 3. "And thy navel is a round cup, which wanteth not mixed drink" [2].

7.2.0.en: The navel is signed with the oil of the Holy Myron in the sacrament of Confirmation (Chrismation), because the Holy Spirit sanctifies the outward members as He sanctifies the inward parts, so that man may be wholly the Lord's.

7.2.1.en: When the Lord spoke with Ezekiel about the ugliness to which man had come and the death that had befallen him, He said of him: "And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut" (Ezek 16:14). For the infant, when it comes out of its mother's womb, must have its navel cut so that it comes out into the light of new life as a living being independent of its mother, no longer needing to be nourished by her blood through the umbilical cord, but begins to practice its humanity to come out to full maturity. In the same way, when the bride and bridegroom enter married life they are bound to have the umbilical cords binding them to their fathers' houses cut, so that they may live the new married life and their mature love may be exercised in the oneness of spirit. I say, thus the Lord Christ sees in His Church that she has entered with Him into married life on a heavenly level, and has cut her navel, so she has become a round cup, that is, has borne the heavenly nature (the circle that has no beginning or end), lacking no mixed drink, for she is no longer in the bowels of the world seeking its outward joys... She has departed, as it were, from her earthly father's house to live in the inner house of the wedding in true satisfaction and sufficiency.

7.3.s.en: 4. "Thy belly is a heap (a pile) of wheat set about with lilies" [3].

7.3.0.en: The Church contains within her storehouses of spiritual food (wheat) that satisfies the soul, in which the Lord Christ dwells, the living Bread which came down from heaven, of which whoever eats shall live forever (Jn 6:51). Thus the Church may appear outwardly poor and hungry, but her bowels are storehouses of good things that satisfy hungry souls, and as the Apostle Paul says: "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Cor 6:10).

7.3.1.en: These good things are surrounded by a hedge of sweet-smelling lilies, as though the fruits of the Church are satisfying and beautiful, drawing souls.

7.4.s.en: 5. "Thy two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle" [3].

7.4.0.en: He had already described her thus in Song 4:5 (which may be consulted).

7.5.s.en: 6. "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory" [4].

7.5.0.en: He had already described her thus: "Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury" (Song 4:4), as steadfast and strong, facing every war, but now He describes her neck as "a tower of ivory," and we have already seen that ivory signifies the acceptance of suffering unto death... for it is taken from the elephant through its sufferings unto death. If the faith of the Church is high as a tower, lifted up toward heaven, she has accepted all ranks of suffering unto death... to remain faithful in her faith, not turning aside after every wind of strange teaching and not being defiled by innovations and heresies; her genuine apostolic faith has cost her a great price!

7.5.1.en: It is a faith of ivory, brilliantly white, with nothing to mar it, and precious!

7.5.2.en: This neck also signifies the chastity and purity of the Church, for she is continually lifting up her head; sin cannot bow it down to the dust or humble her.

7.6.s.en: 7. "Thine eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim" [4].

7.6.0.en: If He had previously described her eyes as the eyes of a dove, in which appears the image of the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies her inner conduct through her continual looking to Him without deviation, He now describes them as the fishponds in Heshbon. This sight reveals the breadth of her insight, for she is like pools open to heaven, which nothing veils from her. This openness toward heaven generates in her an openness toward men also, therefore He called her "fishponds"; everyone who looks at her finds that she contains the fishes within her... not concerned with the things of herself but with those of others (the fishes signify the company of believers)...

7.6.1.en: He does not describe her as springs lest they bear bubbles of air (which signify the hollow life), nor as the sea, for there are no disturbances or anxiety in her, but in the simplicity of faith she lives with a calm spiritual gaze.

7.6.2.en: As for the choice of the city of Heshbon, it is for many reasons, among them:

7.6.3.en: a. "Heshbon" means "reckoning"... So the broad and simple outlook does not mean that man lives without reckoning or without care... but with wisdom he takes into account the counting of the cost.

7.6.4.en: b. The city of Heshbon, now called "Hesban," is the ruins of a city standing on an isolated hill about 16 miles east of the Jordan and about nine miles north of Medeba, standing between the Arnon and the Jabbok. This city was taken by Sihon king of the Amorites as the capital of his kingdom and Moses the prophet gave it to the Reubenites, and it lies on the border dividing the possessions of Reuben and Gad (Num 32:37; Josh 13:26). It is one of the six cities of refuge of the 48 cities given to the Levites (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:66). As though the eyes of the Church or the spiritual insight of the believer are like the calm pools in one of the cities of refuge, to which people flee and enjoy Christ Jesus, the true refuge.

7.6.5.en: c. The city of Heshbon was at the crossroads of the main roads, many multitudes passing through it, and here is a reference to the opening of the believer's heart to many, that they may enjoy the Lord Christ, "the eternal refuge." Therefore the Bridegroom completes His speech, saying: "by the gate of Bath-rabbim." The bath is a unit of measure among the Jews used for liquids, and "rabbim" means "daughter of the multitudes"... as though the believer becomes a son of many multitudes. Or as though man, having enjoyed spiritual insight, calls the multitudes to share this insight with him.

7.7.s.en: 8. "Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus" [4].

7.7.0.en: This expression signifies the nobility of the Church and her holy courage in the truth, and her not fearing falsehood, for though she is meek and humble, she is at the same time strong and mighty.

7.7.1.en: And the nose also signifies the sense of smell for distinguishing between the sweet fragrance of Christ and the passing perfumes of the world. The true believer has a nose like a tower, through which he discerns who is enemy and who is friend, and distinguishes what is for edification and what is for destruction. As for its direction toward Damascus, the commercial city concerned with temporal things, it signifies the boldness of the Church and her ability to face every current.

7.7.2.en: If the believer is bound to have such a nose, how much more is it fitting that the shepherd not be "flat-nosed" (Lev 21:7-21). And as Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [The flat-nosed is he who is unable to discern, for by the sense of smell we distinguish sweet scents from foul. This sense truly signifies the sense of discernment by which we choose virtue and reject vice. Therefore it was said in praise of the Church the bride: "Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon." For the holy Church perceives fully by discernment the trials raised against her for various reasons, and knows beforehand - from above her tower - the battles of evil that are about to occur].

7.8.s.en: 9. "Thine head upon thee is like Carmel,

7.8.0.en: and the hair of thine head like scarlet; the king is held in the galleries" [5].

7.8.1.en: The head of the Church is lifted high like Carmel, the mountain that rises to less than 2000 feet, not in human haughtiness and arrogant self-importance, but in the power of victory over the love of the world and all its storms.

7.8.2.en: And Carmel means "garden land," distinguished by dense greenery and many fruits and forests; so the head of the Church does not appear empty but fruitful, no vain thoughts play in her, but she bears glorious works and offers fruits that satisfy many.

7.8.3.en: Mount Carmel - which was on the southern border of Asher (Josh 19:26) - brings to us glorious and effective memories. There Elijah the prophet stood before the priests of Baal and all the people, asking them not to halt between two opinions: let them serve God or Baal...! And there the priests of Baal were slain (1 Kgs 18:17-40). So when the Church is lifted up toward the heavenly things she does not know halting between the love of God and the love of the world, but kills within her every deviation from the truth, and leads all by the truth.

7.8.4.en: On the top of Carmel Elijah the prophet worshiped and fell to the earth, asking God to give rain upon the land (1 Kgs 18:42-46), and in the Church believers worship with contrition before God that He may rain upon dry hearts with the waters of His grace until they soften with repentance and bring forth the fruit required...

7.8.5.en: And his disciple Elisha the prophet visited Mount Carmel (2 Kgs 2:25), where the widow met him that he might raise her only son from the dead (2 Kgs 4:25)...

7.8.6.en: These are some of our memories on Mount Carmel, to which the head of the Church, lifted above her enemies (Ps 27:6), is likened. As for the hair, we saw before that it signifies the company of believers. It is like scarlet, which is the clothing of kings and also bears the symbol of the blood of the Lord Christ; by our union with the Bridegroom the King, all the members have come to bear the mark of royalty through their sanctification by the precious blood.

7.8.7.en: Before this beautiful, pious sight the Bridegroom says: "the king is held in the galleries," as though He does not want to leave her. This is what the psalmist affirmed by saying: "For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell" (Ps 132:13-14).

7.9.s.en: 10. "How beautiful art thou and how sweet, O my beloved!

7.9.0.en: This is thy greatness in thy delights: this thy stature is like to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters.

7.9.1.en: I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of the high boughs thereof.

7.9.2.en: And thy breasts shall be as clusters of the vine, and the smell of thy nose like apples.

7.9.3.en: And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine, that goeth down sweetly with delight for my beloved, and flows over my lips and my teeth" [6-9].

7.9.4.en: At the conclusion of His description of her He speaks intimately to her: How beautiful art thou?! How sweet art thou?! - according to the original text: "How beautiful hast thou become?!" For the beauty of the Bridegroom was poured out upon her; by His dwelling within her she has acquired a special sweetness! He was mingled with her fruit, which the Lord seeks and finds in her. He looked at her stature and found it like the palm tree, and her breasts like the clusters.

7.9.5.en: Behold, the stature of the Church has appeared; she is like the palm tree, distinguished by its height and uprightness... she has risen to attain the fullness of the stature of Christ (Eph 4:13). And as the psalmist says: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon" (Ps 92:12). Therefore the seventy apostles were symbolized by seventy palm trees (Ex 15:27; Num 33:9), and the house of God was adorned with palm trees (1 Kgs 6:29; Chr 3:5; Ezek 40:22; 41:18), and in eternity believers carry palm branches as a sign of victory (Rev 7). The palm tree with its deep hidden roots meets the springs of living water, and it presents its fruit visibly and beneficially to many, especially in desolate regions... and its branches are used in receiving kings, who wave them as a sign of conquest and victory. As though the heavenly Bridegroom sees in His Church - through her likeness to the palm tree - the hidden deep union with Him, and the fruits offered to the hungry world, and the royal life that is triumphant and victorious!

7.9.6.en: The Bridegroom rejoices in His fruitful bride, so He goes up to the palm tree to gather its fruit. He did not send one of the servants to gather the fruit for Him, but goes up Himself and picks the fruit with His hands; here He declares to the human soul her dignity and greatness, for if for her sake He came down to the world to be united with her, now He goes up upon her... She was lifted up after having been fallen, and by her rising with her Bridegroom to His heavens she shares His glories; He sees Himself going up on His palm tree gathering its fruit, which is in truth the work of His Holy Spirit!

7.9.7.en: He takes hold of its high boughs... as though He sees in her victory a victory for Himself, and in her loftiness a glorification of His saving work. We hold the branches because by the Lord we conquer and triumph. And He holds our victory because it is on His account and for the glory of His holy name. He rejoices and exults in every victory we attain!

7.10.s.en: As for the kinds of fruit, they are:

7.10.0.en: a. He sees her breasts as clusters of the vine... and we have seen that the breasts of the Church are the Old and New Testaments, which stir the spirit of joy in the lives of the believers.

7.10.1.en: b. He sees her nose as apples... and we have seen that the apple is a symbol of the divine Incarnation, as though she continually smells the fragrance of the incarnate God.

7.10.2.en: c. Her throat like the good wine signifies words of continual joy, pleasant and delicious in taste, which make the Bridegroom Himself also rejoice at her joy, so that signs of joy appear on His lips and teeth.

7.10.3.en: When the bride heard the Bridegroom's description and His praise of her, she answered Him: All that You have described me with is from You and for You, O my Beloved.

7.11.0.en: "I am my beloved's (my near one's), and his desire is toward me" [10].

7.11.1.en: In the second chapter, when the bride looked at the Crucified One she perceived His love through which the Lord offered Himself to her as Bridegroom, and she offered her life as His possession... saying: "My beloved (my near one) is mine, and I am his: the Shepherd among the lilies" (Song 2:16).

7.11.2.en: And in the fifth chapter she asks Him to enter His garden, that is, her heart, to accept her love for Him and to receive her life with all her inner energies as a response of love to His work with her, saying: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: the Shepherd among the lilies" (Song 6:3). But here she has risen to eternity, not to offer her life to Him in response to His love but to disclose, on the level of openness and infinity, the extent of His longing for her: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." As though she says to Him... I have come to know the secret of Your praise of me, that You ask me to be with You and for You, to be the object of Your longing forever!

7.11.3.en: This time she does not say: "my beloved is mine," for she was amazed before His delight in her and His longing toward her... He "hath desired Zion for his habitation" (Ps 132:13)...

7.12.0.en: Before this love that she discovered in her Bridegroom toward her she began calling Him:

7.13.s.en: "Come, my beloved (my near one), let us go forth into the field;

7.13.0.en: let us lodge in the villages.

7.13.1.en: Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine hath flowered?!

7.13.4.en: There will I give thee my love (my breasts)" [11-12].

7.13.5.en: When the bride perceived His love for her she began asking Him that they might go out together alone to the field and lodge in the villages away from the noise of the city, and gather of the fruits...

7.14.0.en: What field is this to which she called her beloved to go out with her? Perhaps it is the field of divine work, extended over all humanity, of which the Lord Himself said: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest" (Jn 4:35)... If our Lord Himself calls us to work, yet we shall not go out without Him, but with Him and by Him, for He is the owner of the vineyard and He is the One who gives it increase. Regarding this the Apostle Paul says: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase... For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:6-9).

7.14.1.en: Cain went out to the field but not in the company of the Lord; he went out alone, and there he could not bear the righteous Abel but killed him, and when the Lord reproached him in the boldness of evil he answered: "Am I my brother's keeper?!" (Gen 4:9), and He cursed the earth with him and because of him: "And now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand; when thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth." But the bride refuses to go out to the field except with her Bridegroom and by Him, so her heart expands with love for her brother, and she feels responsibility toward him, so the earth is blessed because of her.

7.14.2.en: And perhaps the field reminds us of the loving meeting between Isaac and his bride Rebekah, for he went out to meditate in the field at the eventide and saw his wife coming on a camel... and she, when she saw him, alighted from the camel and met him... Here the bride longs to go out with Him to the field of contemplations; there her heavenly Bridegroom discloses to her His divine secrets, and she perceives His unspeakable glories; He receives her as His bride forever and she lives in His eternal embrace.

7.14.3.en: And perhaps the bride means by the field "the life of continual striving," for the book of Proverbs says: "He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread" (Prov 12:11)... for the soul has no ability to strive to be satisfied unless the Lord works with her and in her.

7.15.0.en: The bride says: "let us go forth..."

7.15.1.en: In the Lord's speech to His bride and His praise of her she discovered a truth she had not previously perceived in its fullness... that God is not a hard idea isolated in heaven, as Aristotle said of Him that He moved the world and stopped to control it, but rather God is always in motion in His dealing with man. God is a love that is not isolated, who came out to us leaving His glories for a time so that we would not fear and dread Him but love Him and accept Him... He came out to us and dwelt among us. For our sake He became a servant! He also went out outside the camp bearing our shame on His shoulders! And here we see Him going out to us, not disclosing Himself to us that we may love Him, but declaring in us a beauty which is in truth the reflection of His beauty upon us and the fruit of His love that besieges us. And now the soul calls upon Him, saying "let us go forth...," as though she has perceived that without Him she remains a prisoner of "herself," living captive in her shell, asking only for what is for herself. It is a supplication, indeed a cry of love, in which the soul begs her Bridegroom to release her from herself to live with Him in the field of love, asking what is for others.

7.15.2.en: This is a living picture of true married life, for neither party seeks to imprison the other within himself, consuming him for his own account... but while opening the heart to bring the other into it, both go forth together in a unitive love in which each esteems the other as a living independent being. In other words, we often see one of the spouses in his love for the other asking what is for himself, and seeing in the other party not a person living with him on the level of sharing but a "thing" in which he delights, and he stifles his breath and exploits him to satisfy his psychological, social, and biological needs. In his love for the other party he smothers the other's will, freedom, and humanity... supposing that by this he loves him!

7.15.3.en: So when the bride opens her heart to the Bridegroom to enter her, she does not seek Him "to consume Him," if this expression is correct, or as St. John Chrysostom says "to exploit Him," wanting in her Bridegroom to shape Him as she wants, who responds to all her requests and satisfies all her needs and solves all her problems and merely blesses all her actions... But it is fitting that she go out from herself, go out with Him and by Him, so she asks of Him Himself first and submits to His will, and if she asks Him anything and requests a solution of her problems or a blessing for her work, it is only as a fruit of their meeting together, not as the goal of this meeting. In other words: God first in her life... she loves Him for His own sake and not on the level of benefit!

7.16.s.en: Let us lodge in the villages:

7.16.0.en: What are these villages in which she wants to lodge with her Bridegroom?! 1. Perhaps she means by the villages her inner life with its many aspects, as though she says to Him: Come, let us go from the outward appearances of the city and enter my heart and my mind and my emotions and all my inner energies, and lodge with me there, that we may together discover the various fruits of Your Holy Spirit within me; we find the vine has flowered and the pomegranate has blossomed and my breasts offer the milk of pure love. 2. Perhaps here also is a call to serve the villages, for many care for the service of the rich city, but the bride - the Church - is bound to preach and to care within the villages, where the simple and the poor are also. 3. Here is the call to lodge with Him in "many" villages, that is, to accompany Him from village to village, and her heart does not rest in the city or in any one village, but enters with her Bridegroom into the life of union through her service in every place... So the believer does not find the fullness of his rest until his inner depths are at ease concerning all humanity. In the first chapter (Song 1:6) the soul reproached the daughters of Jerusalem that they had made her keeper of the vineyards, but now she is the one who asks to rise early to the many vineyards... She has come out of every selfishness and every closedness to rise early to the vineyards of others, working in them with the Lord, the genuine Vinedresser. And the wonder is that not only has her heart expanded to serve others, but she hastens the service: "let us get up early...". She has realized that the time is short and the days are evil (Eph 5:16).

7.16.1.en: Finally the bride says "there will I give thee my love (my breasts)"... there in the field of service, in the Lord's field, in the villages, in the vineyards, when she offers to humanity her union with Christ her Bridegroom, she is offering to the Lord her love, or offering her breasts (the two Testaments), offering the word of God as the satisfying nourishment for souls.

7.18.0.en: and at our gates are all manner of precious things (fruits), new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved" [13].

7.18.1.en: The mandrake is one of the most beautiful flowers that signify the marital union between a man and his wife, therefore a dispute arose because of it between Rachel and Leah (Gen 30:14)... But the bride concludes her speech by saying that the fragrance of the unitive or marital love between the heavenly Bridegroom and His bride has wafted forth, and the time has come for the perfection of this union.

7.18.2.en: This union whose fragrance has appeared bears precious fruits, which come new every day and old, that is, genuine and deep... they are the fruits of the word of God working in the souls of the believers. These precious fruits appeared at the gates of the believers, who are members of the holy bride.

7.18.3.en: This is what the bride, the mother, offers to Christ the eternal Bridegroom... she offers the fruits of her members by the Holy Spirit!
